Neonatal sea otters (Enhydra lutris) emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 1,868 grams [Wwb = approximately 1,868 grams], a substantial mass for a mustelid neonate that reflects their highly precocial developmental trajectory. Newborn pups are born with a dense coat of natal fur that provides essential thermal insulation in the cold marine environment, and their eyes are open at birth, allowing for immediate visual bonding with the mother. The gestation period that precedes this live birth has been documented to last 140 days [tg = 140 days] at the species' core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that is relatively protracted for a carnivore of this body size. This extended gestation is thought to facilitate the advanced neurological and physiological development observed in the newborn, enabling the pup to be carried and nursed on the mother's chest while she forages. The large birth mass, representing roughly seven percent of the maternal weight, imposes a significant energetic demand during the final trimester of pregnancy and is an adaptation linked to the necessity for the pup to remain buoyant and thermoregulate independently from birth.

A female sea otter typically gives birth to a single pup per reproductive event [N_R_i = single pup per reproductive event], and available field data indicate that she can produce at most one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], making this one of the lowest annual reproductive outputs among marine mammals of comparable size. This maximum reproductive rate, expressed as a single pup per litter and one litter annually, is a direct consequence of the extensive maternal investment required to raise a dependent offspring through a prolonged period of lactation and care, all measured at the species' core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The pup begins nursing immediately after parturition (175 days after parturition) [tx = 175 days after parturition] at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], and this milk-dependent stage continues until the young sea otter achieves nutritional independence. The timing of weaning is critical, as the pup must have developed sufficient diving and foraging skills to locate and handle hard-shelled invertebrate prey before maternal provisioning ceases. Females exhibit strong fidelity to their pups, carrying them on their bellies for the first several weeks and leaving them floating on the water surface, wrapped in kelp, only when diving to forage.

Juvenile sea otters undergo a period of rapid somatic growth after weaning, gradually increasing in body mass as they develop the foraging proficiency necessary for independent survival. The wet weight at weaning has been measured at 13,425 grams [Wwx = 13,425 grams], a value that is more than seven times the neonatal mass and reflects the substantial nutritional transfer that occurred during the nursing interval. The suckling stage, defined as the interval between birth and the cessation of milk provisioning, lasts approximately 175 days [tx = approximately 175 days] at the species' core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This substantial period of maternal investment allows the pup to acquire the complex foraging skills, including tool use for opening hard-shelled prey, that are essential for post-weaning survival in the nearshore marine environment. During this period, the mother gradually introduces her offspring to solid food, often sharing prey items that she has caught and broken open, thereby facilitating the transition from a completely milk-based diet to one composed entirely of marine invertebrates.

As female sea otters approach reproductive maturity, they undergo significant physiological changes that prepare the body for the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. The time since birth at puberty for females has been determined to be 974 days [tp = 974 days], meaning that a young female born in a given year will typically experience her first oestrus around two and a half years of age. at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]This maturational milestone, measured at the species' core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], marks the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to ovulate, although first reproduction in the wild is often deferred until the subsequent breeding season due to the need to acquire a territory and attain sufficient body condition. Puberty in male sea otters occurs somewhat later, generally around three to four years of age, reflecting the different reproductive strategies and competitive demands between the sexes. The attainment of sexual maturity represents a pivotal life-history transition, after which females allocate a substantial portion of their energy budget to successive cycles of pregnancy, parturition, and prolonged lactation that can span nearly two years for a single offspring.

The maximum recorded longevity for the sea otter, based on long-term field studies of tagged individuals in Alaska and California, is 27 years [am = 27 years] when measured at the species' core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This substantial lifespan, comparable to that of other long-lived mustelids such as the wolverine, allows for a protracted reproductive window during which a female can successfully rear multiple pups over her lifetime. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult male has been recorded at 25,850 grams [Wwi = 25,850 grams], making it one of the heaviest members of the family Mustelidae, while adult females are typically smaller, reaching an ultimate wet weight approximately 30 percent less than males. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is linked to the intense male-male competition for access to receptive females during the breeding season. In their natural environment, sea otters face relatively few sources of natural mortality beyond predation by killer whales and white sharks, with senescence-related deaths and the energetic exhaustion of old, post-reproductive females contributing to the age structure of wild populations.
